title: Target-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
claim: Updates differ in how well the lagging target agrees with the online estimate, and a score can quantify this alignment.
layout: 4 small arrow panels left, 2 heatmaps right, shared colorbar
description: The left half is a 2x2 grid of small boxed panels labeled I. Perfect alignment, II. Offline undershoot, III. Offline overshoot and IV. Misalignment. Each box has a vertical gray line marking the current estimate. A red arrow (online error) and a black arrow (offline error) start from that line. In I the arrows are equal, in II and III one is shorter or longer than the other, and in IV they point in opposite directions. A legend underneath explains the colors. The right half has two square heatmaps with online TD error on the x-axis and offline TD error on the y-axis. They share a red-to-green colorbar from 0 to 1. The first, 'Base Alignment Score', is green along the diagonal and red near the horizontal axis. The second, 'Alignment Score', is saturated green in the quadrants where the signs agree. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps.
caption: Left: Stylized visualization of alignment scenarios. We distinguish between updates fully supported by the online network (I and II) and updates that are only partially or not at all supported by the online network (III and IV). Right: Visualization of base alignment and alignment as a function of online and offline temporal difference error.
abstract: Many value-based deep reinforcement learning algorithms rely on target networks - lagged copies of the online network - to stabilize training. While effective, this mechanism introduces a fundamental stability-recency trade-off: slower target updates improve stability but reduce the recency of learning signals, hindering convergence speed. We propose Target-Aligned Reinforcement Learning (TARL), a simple drop-in refinement for existing algorithms that emphasizes transitions for which the target and online network estimates are highly aligned. By focusing updates on well-aligned targets, TARL mitigates the adverse effects of stale target estimates while retaining the stabilizing benefits of target networks. We empirically demonstrate consistent improvements within discrete and continuous control algorithms across various benchmark environments without any hyperparameter tuning, including a 38.18% median peak score gain on Atari-10, while incurring less than a 4% increase in wall-clock time.
